[All Stories](/archive) - [Podcast](/podcast-research-matters) - [Media Relations](/media-relations) - [Cornellians](https://alumni.cornell.edu/cornellians/) # Cornell mathematicians win grants to ensure AI safety, research integrity ## By [Kate Blackwood](mailto:cunews@cornell.edu "Email Kate Blackwood") [College of Arts and Sciences](https://as.cornell.edu/) September 2026 was a watershed month for the field of mathematics, as OpenAI claimed to solve the Navier-Stokes problem with artificial intelligence (AI), Fields Medal winners branched into AI safety and spoke up for AI constraints, and prominent mathematicians, including Cornell professors Steven Strogatz and Lionel Levine, commented in the media on the benefits and risks of AI. As mathematicians work through challenges related to AI, Cornell math faculty members are leading the field with work integrating AI into math and mathematics into AI. [Levine](https://math.cornell.edu/lionel-levine), professor of mathematics in the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S), was awarded $1.5 million over 18 months from the nonprofit [Coefficient Giving](https://coefficientgiving.org/) to research AI safety. [Daniel Halpern-Leistner](https://math.cornell.edu/daniel-halpern-leistner), associate professor of mathematics (A&S), was awarded $2.3 million over three years to create tools incorporating AI to allow formalization of mathematics, which involves computer verification, from the [Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency](https://www.darpa.mil/) (DARPA). Mathematics department chair [Tara Holm](https://math.cornell.edu/tara-holm), professor of mathematics (A&S), says the grants are timely at a moment of publicity for the intersection of math and AI. “The mathematics community is grappling with how our discipline will evolve with the advent of AI tools,” Holm said. “Lionel and Daniel are working at the forefront of these questions and are poised to play a major role as the field progresses.” With the Coefficient Giving grant, Levine is building mathematical tools for AI safety by focusing on understanding and evaluating the “constitution” that determines a frontier language model’s characters and values. highlights.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Two former Groq engineers have filed a lawsuit in Delaware's Court of Chancery alleging that Nvidia's $20 billion asset deal with the AI chip startup unfairly squeezed out common stockholders. The complaint claims Groq's board approved the transaction without a required stockholder vote and that $17 billion of the deal value went to a non-exclusive technology license while another $3 billion was reserved for employee stock awards. Groq has called the lawsuit meritless and said it will defend itself vigorously. Nvidia has not commented on the litigation. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers](https://img.biggo.com/0wAiLEjI8NkcbWSTvFfEa_460KUCeiIqgozG7i8w6OM/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2NjMGJlMGFlLWY3ZmQtNDFjZC1iNjU3LWYzMWQ0YWExZjVmM18xNzkxMjUxMTA0X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is facing a legal challenge over its $20 billion asset agreement with AI chip designer Groq, after two former engineers at the startup alleged that stockholders were squeezed out at an unfairly low price. Joshua Rubin and Benjamin Serebrin filed the complaint on Oct. 2 in Delaware's Court of Chancery. Both had departed Groq before the Nvidia transaction was announced, according to their LinkedIn profiles, but the lawsuit states they continued to hold equity in the company. The case marks the first significant legal test of a deal structure that has drawn scrutiny for how it allocates value between technology licenses, employee compensation, and common stockholders. The dispute traces back to a December licensing agreement that granted Nvidia access to Groq's inference technology, which is used to run trained AI models efficiently. As part of that arrangement, Groq founder and CEO Jonathan Ross and President Sunny Madra joined Nvidia, along with other senior executives. The lawsuit indicates that roughly 150 to 200 Groq engineers also became Nvidia employees in connection with the transaction. Groq, for its part, has maintained that it will continue operating as an independent company and has raised approximately $1 billion since June from investors that include Nvidia itself. The core of the complaint centers on how the $20 billion was divided. The plaintiffs allege that Nvidia assigned $17 billion to a license described as non-exclusive, while another $3 billion was reserved in Nvidia restricted stock units for Groq employees who moved with the technology. The lawsuit further claims that investment funds with representatives on Groq's board were positioned to capture windfall returns from what the plaintiffs describe as a later squeeze-out transaction. "A Board majority was conflicted as a result," the complaint states, adding that "the Board's conflicted choice cost Groq's stockholders billions of dollars." The former engineers argue that Groq's directors "sold the company to Nvidia without the stockholder vote Delaware law requires and without any process designed to test or maximize the value of what Nvidia bought." Groq has forcefully rejected the allegations. A company spokesperson said the licensing agreement "delivered exceptional value for Groq, our investors, and our employees." The spokesperson added that the lawsuit "is meritless and we will vigorously defend ourselves against it," while emphasizing that the company remains focused on serving customers and building what it describes as the world's leading AI inference cloud. highlights.content: © 2026 Cybernews – Latest Cybersecurity and Tech News, Research & Analysis. # Germany’s sovereign AI model Kolibri challenges US and Chinese rivals Built in Germany from scratch. ![The logo of Kolibri and German flag between 2 green cabinets with drawers](https://media.cybernews.com/images/featured-big/2026/10/germany-kolibri-model.jpg) Image by Insaanu Studio via Unsplash/Illustration by Cybernews ![Eglė Krištopaitytė](data:image/svg+xml;charset%3D'utf-8',%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%2040%2040'%2F%3E) ![](/images/follow-us/google-g.png) Key Takeaways by [nexos.ai](https://nexos.ai), reviewed by Cybernews staff. **The new open-weight large language model (LLM), designed for public administration, is outperforming competitors from Alibaba and Nvidia.** The Heidelberg-based AI startup Aleph Alpha released Kolibri on October 3rd, 2026, which is German Unity Day. Kolibri is an English-German Mixture-of-Experts Transformer, meaning it is divided into separate sub-networks called “experts.” The model uses 3.46 billion active parameters per token, out of 78.1B total. The model was specifically built for “sovereign mission-critical work” in regulated areas, including public administration, industrials, and aerospace, taking into account their particular “domain-specific language, regulatory, and procedural realities.” ## More from Cybernews ![A mascot for Meta's AI agent Muse](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/meta-muse-privacy.jpg) ![claude-logo-getty](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude.jpg) ![Anthropic logo](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude-pentagon.jpg) ![Ray-Ban Meta glasses](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/07/RaybamAIglasses.jpg) ![arXiv AI](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/shutterstock_2400385601.jpg) ![Tavus HIM model Griffin](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/tavus_griffin.gif) The company says Kolibri’s small, efficient size allows it to run on-premises without sending internal data to third-party inference services. Kolibri complies with the EU AI Act, the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), according to Aleph Alpha, with “copyright law being a focus of our work to trustworthy technology.” The model was built in Germany and trained on infrastructure in Germany and Finland, under the law of these countries. It was specifically trained to answer “I don’t know” when it cannot provide an answer, reducing the risk of hallucinations. [Kolibri was developed as a German and English bilingual model](https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/), including organic German data – 21.3% of the pre-training tokens are German. “We started the year with the conviction that Europe needs its own sovereign AI. Built in Germany from scratch and on infrastructure in Europe specifically for our customers,” Aleph Alpha’s X post reads. ## Kolibri vs American and Chinese models Aleph Alpha compared Kolibri to 3 other open-weight models with up to 4 times its active parameter count: Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6-35B-A3B, Mistral Small 4 119B-A6B, and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B. Kolibri outperformed all rivals across mathematical reasoning in both German and English (AIME 2025 and 2026 benchmark), deep reasoning (GPQA diamond), and code (LiveCodeBench v6). The model also showed superiority across benchmarks assessing an AI agent’s ability to find and navigate through large amounts of information. Kolibri, however, fell behind Qwen’s 3.6-35B-A3B across long-context comprehension and retrieval. ## Where to download Kolibri? The model can be downloaded from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1) and used under the Apache 2.0 license terms. Nvidia Is Becoming an Inference Fight, Not a Chip Fight The next big AI chip battle may not be about who trains the biggest model. It could be about who can make [AI respond fastest](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/10/62118140/ai-stocks-bubble-earnings) once the model is already built. That is putting **Cerebras Systems Inc.** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS)[CBRS](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS)) and **Nvidia Corp** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/NVDA)[NVDA](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/NVDA)) on opposite sides of an increasingly valuable fight over AI inference. ## Altman Reassures Cerebras Investors Cerebras shares climbed more than 7% in early trading Monday after **OpenAI** CEO **Sam Altman** pushed back against speculation that the chipmaker had lost a key role at OpenAI. "Cerebras is a close partner, and we have a deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed," Altman [said](https://x.com/sama/status/2106147184693620924?s=20) in a post on X. The comments came days after Cerebras shares fell nearly 20% after a SemiAnalysis [report](https://lnkd.in/p/gU9ai9Z2) said OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast tier ran on Nvidia GPUs rather than Cerebras hardware. The report raised an obvious question for investors: If OpenAI is turning to Nvidia for its fastest AI experience, where does that leave Cerebras? The answer may be more nuanced than a single model or a single customer deployment. OpenAI and Cerebras announced a multiyear agreement in January for 750 megawatts of Cerebras inference capacity through 2028. OpenAI said at the time that Cerebras would add a dedicated low-latency solution to its compute portfolio, with the goal of delivering faster responses across workloads. ## Speed Is Becoming a Market That distinction matters because inference is what happens after an AI model has been trained: It is the computing required every time a user asks a question, generates code or interacts with an AI agent. Cerebras has built its investment case around making that process faster. The company said in August that its cloud business grew 281% year over year, while data-center capacity live or under contract surpassed 600 megawatts. It also said manufacturing capacity was set to increase more than 10 times in 2026. Now Wall Street is putting a number behind that opportunity. Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh estimates the fast-inference market could reach $550 billion by 2030, representing roughly 20% of AI workloads. He reiterated an Outperform rating and [$300 price target](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS/price-targets) on CBRS Monday. It lies in rethinking the systems that make up the server rooms, by [Gianni Rusconi](https://argomenti.ilsole24ore.com/gianni-rusconi.html) [![](/static/img/icon-google--g.svg)Aggiungi Il Sole 24 Ore ai preferiti su Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=ilsole24ore.com) 6' min read Translated by AI For feedback, please contact [english@ilsole24ore.com](mailto:english@ilsole24ore.com?body=https://en.ilsole24ore.com/art/data-centres-what-they-are-like-today-and-what-they-will-be-like-in-five-years-time-AJ3MWHZB) [Versione italiana](https://www.ilsole24ore.com/art/i-data-center-l-ai-come-sono-oggi-e-come-saranno-cinque-anni-AJ3MWHZB) 6' min read Translated by AI For feedback, please contact [english@ilsole24ore.com](mailto:english@ilsole24ore.com?body=https://en.ilsole24ore.com/art/data-centres-what-they-are-like-today-and-what-they-will-be-like-in-five-years-time-AJ3MWHZB) [Versione italiana](https://www.ilsole24ore.com/art/i-data-center-l-ai-come-sono-oggi-e-come-saranno-cinque-anni-AJ3MWHZB) ZAGREB – Artificial intelligence is reshaping data centres, and this process of change ranges from rack density to the systems that supply power and dissipate heat. The issue is well known: infrastructure is required to support heavier workloads and ensure ever-faster processing cycles, whilst projects involving the use of AI are growing in scale. Part of the solution is built in the factory, whilst other aspects concern technologies for cooling and controlling the systems, with liquid-cooling solutions and digital tools becoming increasingly prevalent. highlights.content: UPDATED 20:46 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Reflection AI debuts open-source Beam model with 501B parameters Reflection AI Inc. today introduced Beam, an open-source large language model with 501 billion parameters. The launch comes a few months after the startup raised funding at a $25 billion valuation. Around the same time, Reflection AI reportedly inked a $6.3 billion deal with SpaceX Corp. to rent Nvidia GB300 NVL72 appliances. It used those systems, which each contain 72 graphics cards, to train Beam. Reflection AI benchmarked its model against GLM-5.2, an open-source LLM that includes about 250 billion more parameters. The company determined that Beam can perform some tasks better while using between one third and one fourth the hardware. Furthermore, it says that the LLM approaches the performance of Qwen 3.8-Max, a model with over 2 trillion parameters. The launch is particularly notable because many of the open-source ecosystem’s most advanced LLMs were created by Chinese companies. That includes Qwen 3.8-Max and GLM-5.2. Beam is the first open-source model from a U.S. startup to have demonstrated comparable or better performance. However, free LLMs continue to trail frontier models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.1. Reflection AI kicked off the development of Beam by training a relatively small prototype model. It then created a series of successively larger, more capable algorithms. The workflow eventually produced Beam Base, the foundation on which Beam is based. Reflection AI developed Beam Base using a cluster of 6,144 graphics cards. It trained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens sourced from the public web and commercial sources. According to Reflection AI, that dataset included a significant amount of software code. The company created custom filters for each programming language to remove low-quality files. Reflection AI developed Beam Base in under four weeks. It subsequently performed midtraining, an optimization process that extended the model’s context window and enhanced its reasoning capabilities. That phase of the project set the stage for the third, most hardware-intensive phase of the training workflow. Reflection AI spun up 10,000 GB300 graphics cards and used them to launch 1.3 billion reinforcement learning sandboxes. Those are virtual environments in which an AI model learns new skills. Beam’s sandboxes were optimized for tasks such as generating code, searching the web and running AI agents. Reflection AI says that the project’s reinforcement learning phase took only four weeks. The company avoided unnecessary delays by developing software that prevented malfunctions from interrupting the workflow. According to Reflection AI, its cluster achieved a median recovery time of eight minutes across the 71 errors that cropped up during training. Beam is initially available through an early access program. highlights.content: # Kolibri, a sovereign AI model built for free and for mission-critical national tasks, is open source and transparent in its development process, intended for use in regulated fields such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00.png) German AI startup Aleph Alpha announced a new language model called ' **Kolibri** ' on October 3, 2026, which is German Unity Day. **Kolibri Has Landed: A Sovereign Open-Weight Model — Aleph Alpha** <https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/> One of Kolibri's key features is its efficient design, which limits the number of active parameters to 3 billion despite having a total of 78 billion parameters. At the time of its announcement, it supports English and German and context lengths of up to 1 million tokens. Furthermore, its sophisticated training pipeline automates the entire process from data ingestion, curation, ablation, pre-training, post-training, and final evaluation, enabling hundreds of experiments and stable pre-training without manual intervention even in the event of hardware failures or data connectivity issues. Kolibri is intended for use in highly regulated and mission-critical sectors such as public administration, industry, and aerospace, and it excels particularly in German language processing capabilities, reasoning, mathematics, agent behavior, and features optimized for customer-specific use cases. Kolibri optimizes the trade-off between model performance and deployment cost by using only 3 billion active parameters out of a total of 78 billion parameters for each token processing. The graph below shows the processing performance of various open models in English and German. The horizontal axis represents processing speed, and the vertical axis represents the benchmark score. In both English and German, Kolibri has secured the position of 'highest performance compared to models with the same speed.' [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01.png) Benchmark results show Kolibri performing comparably to models with up to four times the number of active parameters, such as Nemotron 3 Super, in mathematical, coding, grounding, and long-text context tasks. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02.png) Regarding sovereignty and compliance considerations, Aleph Alpha defines 'sovereignty' from two perspectives: 'how the model is built' and 'how it is transferred to the customer.' Regarding model construction, they prioritize transparency in weighting and curation, making the decision-making process behind development visible, and explaining how the model arrived at a specific answer through its inference trajectory. Furthermore, Aleph Alpha's proprietary Merlin-Arthur protocol ensures model reliability, so Kolibri refrains from answering and reduces hallucination if the context does not support the answer. The model is built in Germany, and training is conducted without foreign control throughout the entire pipeline, from data curation to pre- and post-training and optimization in the model factory, on German and Finnish infrastructure, in accordance with European and German law. This end-to-end pipeline management is the foundation supporting model sovereignty, and by transferring management rights to the customer, they gain complete deployment flexibility and enable controllable inference processing to trade off cost and latency with answer quality. AI Agents.content: Posted: # Researchers are tracking a Chinese AI ‘agent fleet’ A new fleet of AI agents is making its presence felt on the Internet. On Sunday, a group of independent researchers posted preliminary findings about the agents, observing that they seem to be running on Tencent’s infrastructure and targeting Alibaba’s map service, Amap. Researchers, however, resisted the term “swarm,” noting that there seems to be little coordination between their different queries. “‘Agent fleet,’ not ‘swarm:’” one researcher wrote in the preliminary report, “many parallel agents on the same kind of task, with no sign of communication between them.” The agents were discovered by monitoring traffic to the domain-scanning service, URLquery, a technique that previously revealed long-running activity by OpenAI agents. AI agents often use URLquery to load websites that they cannot access directly, leaving a record of their activities that can be valuable to researchers. In this case, the record showed queries to Alibaba’s Amap service, seeking directions to different entrances of various public places, including a park, a zoo, and a hospital. The research is ongoing and so few details are available, but the behavior shows how persistent AI agent activity has become on the internet. In the wake of the Hugging Face incident, many researchers are actively monitoring for rogue agent activity on the internet. Much of that activity has been easy to find because agents tend to use the same techniques and make little effort to conceal themselves. In this case, the agents don’t seem to have been doing anything more nefarious than side-stepping Alibaba’s API rules — but we may not always be so lucky. AI Agents.content: * [Identity & Access Management Security](/cybersecurity-operations/identity-access-management-security) # Agentic AI: Blurring the Human and Non-Human Identity lines Agentic AI challenges identity security. Separate identities won't solve overprivileged users or audit gaps. Strong identity governance is the real foundation. October 5, 2026 15 Min Read Source: Adobe Stock Sponsored by Semperis You can’t have a non-human identity (NHI) discussion these days without bringing up agentic AI. Managing and securing agentic identity is just one of the many ways AI has put the cybersecurity industry in a gap. The security standards that exist today do not directly address what we need to cope with the accelerated proliferation of agents in our identity systems. Historically, NHI conversations were rooted in questions like, “How do we inventory, manage, and secure all our service accounts?” Now, the conversation focuses on questions like, “Do we give AI its own identity?” and “How do we tell if an action was taken by a user or their agent?.” Standards bodies are trying to answer these questions with new specifications such as the AAuth Protocol ([currently in draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol/)). However, there are lots of different ideas out there, and standards can take time to progress from inception to reality. Companies such as Microsoft are tackling the issue on a practical level. Microsoft has built Agent ID, a framework for managing agentic identity. Agent ID has sparked a lot of research ([including our own at Semperis)](https://www.semperis.com/category/agentic-ai/?utm_medium=pd&utm_source=informatech) and a lot of industry conversation. However, Agent ID is only practical in certain use cases. (You can learn more in our research team’s blog [here](https://www.semperis.com/blog/understanding-microsoft-agent-identity-platform/?utm_medium=pd&utm_source=informatech).) Related:[Carbonato Botnet Puts an AI Agent on Hacked Docker Hosts](/identity-access-management-security/carbonato-botnet-ai-agent-hacked-docker-hosts) ## When AI borrows the human identity One of the big concerns is what happens when AI, acting as a human (e.g., using the same credentials as a human), goes off the rails. A lot of companies out there are offering AI tools to either detect or (theoretically) block AI actions. However, the bulk of that tooling focuses on an agentic identity that’s an agentic platform or system operating against targets, not AI running on a developer or sysadmin machine and acting on their behalf. And those that focus on the developer scenario require an agent on the system, as they are essentially inspecting user actions in a way similar to EDR platforms. This is the scenario we’re going to break down. We’ll explore how agents really work and intersect with identity—and available approaches to securing them. ## A common scenario Let’s dive into a common scenario: Visual Studio Code with the Claude Code extension installed and a user who has an Azure subscription. The security standards that exist today do not directly address what we need to cope with the accelerated proliferation of agents in our identity systems. Historically, NHI conversations were rooted in questions like, “How do we inventory, manage, and secure all our service accounts?” Now, the conversation focuses on questions like, “Do we give AI its own identity?” and “How do we tell if an action was taken by a user or their agent?.” Standards bodies are trying to answer these questions with new specifications such as the AAuth Protocol ([currently in draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol/)). The White House Accord on Super Intelligence was signed on September 29 by executives from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and NVIDIA. This agreement aims to address growing concerns surrounding the development and deployment of powerful AI technologies, as first reported by Infosecurity Magazine. The accord outlines four layers of safety controls for companies developing and deploying frontier AI models. These include internal monitoring for model capabilities and alignment, with specific attention to cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, ensuring models do not access systems unintentionally. A second layer involves an internal team to verify the effectiveness of these controls and remediate issues. The third layer mandates independent external audits to assess control functionality. Finally, an independent board committee will oversee these processes and ensure remediation of identified problems. This initiative follows recent disclosures from Anthropic, Meta, and OpenAI regarding their AI models accessing unauthorized systems or exceeding test environments, highlighting the urgent need for robust safety measures in the rapidly evolving AI landscape. LLMs.content: © 2026 Cybernews – Latest Cybersecurity and Tech News, Research & Analysis. # Germany’s sovereign AI model Kolibri challenges US and Chinese rivals Built in Germany from scratch. ![The logo of Kolibri and German flag between 2 green cabinets with drawers](https://media.cybernews.com/images/featured-big/2026/10/germany-kolibri-model.jpg) Image by Insaanu Studio via Unsplash/Illustration by Cybernews ![Eglė Krištopaitytė](data:image/svg+xml;charset%3D'utf-8',%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%2040%2040'%2F%3E) ![](/images/follow-us/google-g.png) Key Takeaways by [nexos.ai](https://nexos.ai), reviewed by Cybernews staff. **The new open-weight large language model (LLM), designed for public administration, is outperforming competitors from Alibaba and Nvidia.** The Heidelberg-based AI startup Aleph Alpha released Kolibri on October 3rd, 2026, which is German Unity Day. Kolibri is an English-German Mixture-of-Experts Transformer, meaning it is divided into separate sub-networks called “experts.” The model uses 3.46 billion active parameters per token, out of 78.1B total. It was specifically trained to answer “I don’t know” when it cannot provide an answer, reducing the risk of hallucinations. [Kolibri was developed as a German and English bilingual model](https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/), including organic German data – 21.3% of the pre-training tokens are German. “We started the year with the conviction that Europe needs its own sovereign AI. LLMs.content: UPDATED 20:46 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Reflection AI debuts open-source Beam model with 501B parameters Reflection AI Inc. today introduced Beam, an open-source large language model with 501 billion parameters. The launch comes a few months after the startup raised funding at a $25 billion valuation. Around the same time, Reflection AI reportedly inked a $6.3 billion deal with SpaceX Corp. to rent Nvidia GB300 NVL72 appliances. It used those systems, which each contain 72 graphics cards, to train Beam. Reflection AI benchmarked its model against GLM-5.2, an open-source LLM that includes about 250 billion more parameters. The company determined that Beam can perform some tasks better while using between one third and one fourth the hardware. Furthermore, it says that the LLM approaches the performance of Qwen 3.8-Max, a model with over 2 trillion parameters. The launch is particularly notable because many of the open-source ecosystem’s most advanced LLMs were created by Chinese companies. That includes Qwen 3.8-Max and GLM-5.2. Beam is the first open-source model from a U.S. startup to have demonstrated comparable or better performance. However, free LLMs continue to trail frontier models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.1. Reflection AI kicked off the development of Beam by training a relatively small prototype model. It then created a series of successively larger, more capable algorithms. The workflow eventually produced Beam Base, the foundation on which Beam is based. Reflection AI developed Beam Base using a cluster of 6,144 graphics cards. It trained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens sourced from the public web and commercial sources. According to Reflection AI, that dataset included a significant amount of software code. The company created custom filters for each programming language to remove low-quality files. Reflection AI developed Beam Base in under four weeks. It subsequently performed midtraining, an optimization process that extended the model’s context window and enhanced its reasoning capabilities. That phase of the project set the stage for the third, most hardware-intensive phase of the training workflow. Reflection AI spun up 10,000 GB300 graphics cards and used them to launch 1.3 billion reinforcement learning sandboxes. Those are virtual environments in which an AI model learns new skills. Beam’s sandboxes were optimized for tasks such as generating code, searching the web and running AI agents. Reflection AI says that the project’s reinforcement learning phase took only four weeks. The company avoided unnecessary delays by developing software that prevented malfunctions from interrupting the workflow. According to Reflection AI, its cluster achieved a median recovery time of eight minutes across the 71 errors that cropped up during training. Beam is initially available through an early access program. Reflection AI plans to release its weights, documentation and fine-tuning tools later this month. ##### Photo of Reflection AI founders Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou: Lightspeed # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. LLMs.content: # Kolibri, a sovereign AI model built for free and for mission-critical national tasks, is open source and transparent in its development process, intended for use in regulated fields such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00.png) German AI startup Aleph Alpha announced a new language model called ' **Kolibri** ' on October 3, 2026, which is German Unity Day. **Kolibri Has Landed: A Sovereign Open-Weight Model — Aleph Alpha** <https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/> One of Kolibri's key features is its efficient design, which limits the number of active parameters to 3 billion despite having a total of 78 billion parameters. At the time of its announcement, it supports English and German and context lengths of up to 1 million tokens. Furthermore, its sophisticated training pipeline automates the entire process from data ingestion, curation, ablation, pre-training, post-training, and final evaluation, enabling hundreds of experiments and stable pre-training without manual intervention even in the event of hardware failures or data connectivity issues. Kolibri is intended for use in highly regulated and mission-critical sectors such as public administration, industry, and aerospace, and it excels particularly in German language processing capabilities, reasoning, mathematics, agent behavior, and features optimized for customer-specific use cases. Kolibri optimizes the trade-off between model performance and deployment cost by using only 3 billion active parameters out of a total of 78 billion parameters for each token processing. The graph below shows the processing performance of various open models in English and German. The horizontal axis represents processing speed, and the vertical axis represents the benchmark score. In both English and German, Kolibri has secured the position of 'highest performance compared to models with the same speed.' [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01.png) Benchmark results show Kolibri performing comparably to models with up to four times the number of active parameters, such as Nemotron 3 Super, in mathematical, coding, grounding, and long-text context tasks. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02.png) Regarding sovereignty and compliance considerations, Aleph Alpha defines 'sovereignty' from two perspectives: 'how the model is built' and 'how it is transferred to the customer.' LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) ![GitHub releases ReviewBench, an open benchmark for evaluating AI code review agents](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fgithub-releases-reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-evaluating-ai-code-review-agents-1_1791218337209-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #AI # GitHub releases ReviewBench, an open benchmark for evaluating AI code review agents • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •6 min read Share this article GitHub launched ReviewBench, a public benchmark for measuring how well AI code review tools catch real issues in pull requests. The benchmark draws on 219 pull requests across 19 languages and validated its scoring system with a 96.6% agreement rate among senior engineers. AI code review has become a standard part of many development workflows. Tools inspect pull requests, flag potential issues, and help teams decide what deserves attention before code ships. The problem: measuring which reviewer performs best at what task. A reviewer that surfaces many issues may also produce noise, while one tuned for precision may miss critical bugs. GitHub released ReviewBench on Oct. 5, 2026, an open benchmark designed to evaluate AI code review systems on real-world pull requests. The benchmark supports breakdowns by severity and category, publishes its evaluation rubric and judge model, and tracks how offline scores predict production experiment outcomes. ## What ReviewBench includes ReviewBench contains 219 public pull requests drawn from 187 open source repositories spanning 19 languages. GitHub modeled the benchmark's language and repository-size distributions after 103.9 million real GitHub pull requests. The team weighted pull request size toward the middle and end of the distribution, reducing the share of tiny single-file changes where review quality matters less. TypeScript appears in 68 pull requests, Python in 41, C# in 25, Go in 19, and JavaScript in 15. The remaining 51 pull requests cover other languages. Pull requests add or remove 50 lines or fewer in 17 cases, 51 to 200 lines in 40, 201 to 500 lines in 44, 501 to 1,000 lines in 40, and more than 1,000 lines in 78 cases. The full dataset, including pull requests, findings, labels, and severity and category annotations, is publicly available at [reviewbench.github.com](https://reviewbench.github.com). ## How the golden set works A benchmark is only as reliable as its ground truth. ReviewBench builds its golden set through three stages. First, the team gathers candidate findings from multiple sources: real human reviewers, issues inferred from author follow-up commits, deterministic analysis tools, and frontier large language models across different model families. Second, they semantically deduplicate findings that identify the same underlying issue. Third, they validate each finding under a shared rubric. A finding counts as a true positive only when it is true, relevant, and non-trivial. The source of a finding does not determine its validity. Claude Sonnet 5 serves as the LLM grader, applying a consistent evaluation rubric across all submissions. GitHub publishes both the rubric and the judge used to apply it. ## Six metrics, two families Most benchmarks report precision and recall against a fixed golden set. ReviewBench reports six metrics in two families. Grounded precision, grounded recall, and grounded F1 score use only existing gold-set labels. They answer a direct question: of the issues the benchmark already knows about, how many did the agent find, and what share of the agent's findings matched a known issue? Augmented precision, recall, and F1 score also evaluate findings that match nothing in the golden set. The judge independently determines whether those unmatched findings are true or false positives. This gives an agent credit for valid issues that no producer in the golden set surfaced. The distinction matters as ...

LLMs.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # U.S.-China AI Gap Narrows to 3% as DeepSeek Matches Anthropic's Performance [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) According to Bloomberg Intelligence analysis, the benchmark score gap between China's top AI models and their U.S. counterparts has narrowed to just 3% following the release of DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash. The figure, down sharply from 15% at the start of the year, reflects DeepSeek's rise to 6th place globally on LiveBench, where it now performs on par with Anthropic and OpenAI's leading systems. The development raises fundamental questions about the effectiveness of U.S. semiconductor export controls. However, China's AI industry faces a separate challenge: with more than 1,100 large language models competing in a crowded market and intense price competition, profitability before 2030 appears unlikely. Heightened U.S. regulatory scrutiny over distillation allegations adds further uncertainty. ##### Key Elements ![U.S.-China AI Gap Narrows to 3% as DeepSeek Matches Anthropic's Performance](https://img.biggo.com/11egqU8VqhWu8ea8TUqB_0WQvuT6W16JYWvvF9gxE3k/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzMxOGU4NDM2LTU5ZjQtNGZmMS04ZjJkLTg2ZjA1OGNlOTMxNF8xNzkxMTgyMzk1X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) China's artificial intelligence models are closing in on U.S. frontrunners, with the performance gap between the two countries narrowing to a record low of 3%. DeepSeek's latest model, released last month, has been assessed as matching the performance of top-tier systems from Anthropic and OpenAI, fueling growing doubts about the sustainability of U.S. technological dominance. Robert Lea, senior analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said in a report on the 5th that following the release of DeepSeek's "V4.1 Flash," the benchmark score difference between China's best AI models and competing U.S. models stands at just 3%. The gap has narrowed dramatically from roughly 9% in May and 15% at the start of the year. He projected that Chinese companies will continue to expand their market share. DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash ranked 6th globally on LiveBench, an AI model performance evaluation platform. This marks the highest ranking for a Chinese model since DeepSeek first gained attention with its reasoning-specialized "R1" model last year. LiveBench is a benchmark that comprehensively evaluates answer and analysis capabilities across questions, puzzles, and tasks. DeepSeek's latest score of 81.1 points is not far behind Anthropic's top model at 83.4 points. The analyst assessed that DeepSeek demonstrates "comparable performance" to the leading models from Anthropic and OpenAI. However, only three of the top 15 models on LiveBench are Chinese, meaning the results do not yet upend the broader upper echelon. ### Questions Over Export Control Effectiveness China's rapid catch-up is attributed to deepening AI expertise and researchers' growing ability to optimize models for domestically produced semiconductors. This raises fundamental questions about whether U.S. export controls on advanced chips such as Nvidia's are effective in curbing China's AI development and the alternative chip development led by Huawei and others. Lea noted that China's progress "raises bigger questions about the long-term sustainability of U.S. technological dominance in AI." The U.S. and China are engaged in an intense battle for leadership, both viewing AI as a pivotal technology that will determine economic productivity, military superiority, and global influence. In the opening keynote, Unily CEO Lokdeep Singh announced the launch of [Content Studio](https://www.unily.com/content-studio). Described as a “creative engine for enterprise content,” this new standalone offering is intended to help organizations turn trusted source material into tailored content that different audiences can read, watch, listen to, or view without losing the original meaning as content is transformed across formats and channels. ### Content Studio Is The First Standalone Product From Unily Content Studio is an AI-powered content transformation and production engine that allows subject-matter experts to take trusted corporate content sources and transform the underlying information into a variety of “expressions,” such as an explainer video, an infographic, or a podcast designed for specific audiences. Unily product leaders showcased a demo using the scenario of a luxury hotel chain announcing its new company strategy and taking artifacts such as the town hall transcript, a slide deck, and documents in a Unily-based intranet and transforming the message into specific outputs (i.e., an infographic) for a specific audience (e.g., the hotel housekeeping staff). Key capabilities include: * **Grounding in facts.** Only the imported/linked source material is used to generate the content artifacts. Content Studio uses AI to extract the core facts and does not allow the expressions to use any information not found in the approved sources. * **Output to a range of surfaces, with more to come in the future.** Generated content can be pushed into Unily’s intranet platform and further edited in its CMS, but it will also support Microsoft SharePoint and digital signage. Other platforms will be supported based on customer demand. * **Tools to design content for specific audiences within branding guardrails.** Creators can generate projects for specific initiatives, such as the company strategy communication plan or a product launch. Within a project, the creator uploads the trusted sources and can use natural language to get AI to generate a storyboard and images — for example, create a one-page infographic encouraging housekeeping staff to embody the new strategy on their next shift, along with a one-minute video for hotel managers that summarizes key points relevant to their role. * **Brand guardrails.** Content Studio provides a skills library that grounds AI in a specific company voice (i.e., tone, reading level) and defines roles and audiences. While the example skills shown in the mainstage demo were written in markdown language, plain text can also be used to create a new skill. Admins can also define overall branding (e.g., colors, fonts, etc.) and voices for podcast/video expressions that can reflect different genders, tones, or accents. Third-party-licensed voices can be integrated, and Unily partners with a third-party voice AI tool that can generate the voice of a real person — such as an executive — by recording 30 minutes of speaking. AI Product.content: IT Brief UK - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief UK logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg) United Kingdom](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.uk) ![SAS launches AI Navigator for enterprise governance](https://itbrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/10/06/kathy-lange-and-reggie-townsend-story-320643.webp) [SaaS](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/software-as-a-service) [Data governance](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/data-governance) [Risk & Compliance](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/risk-compliance) # SAS launches AI Navigator for enterprise governance Mon, 5th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.co.uk/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) SAS has launched AI Navigator on Microsoft Marketplace, a software tool designed to help companies govern their use of artificial intelligence. The software-as-a-service product is aimed at AI, data, compliance and risk teams that need to track AI use cases, models and agents across an organisation. It gives customers a single view of existing systems, including large language models, AI agents, open-source models and SAS models, without requiring them to change how they build AI. The launch comes as companies face growing pressure to show that AI systems comply with internal rules and external regulation. SAS cited research conducted with IDC that found organisations with strong trust management are 15 times more likely to report strong returns on AI investment. The research also highlighted a practical problem for businesses deploying more autonomous systems. Employees often override AI recommendations when they cannot understand or explain how decisions were made, weakening confidence in the technology and limiting its use. SAS AI Navigator is intended to address that gap by creating an inventory of AI use cases and linking them to governance requirements. The system extends oversight beyond a single application to the underlying model or agent and the policies attached to it. For companies using customer service chatbots, for example, that could mean governing both the use case itself and the underlying model or agent, such as Claude or Microsoft Copilot. Customers can apply internal policies as well as external regulations and frameworks across those deployments. **Policy packs** The product also includes access to policy packs from partners including Protiviti and Asenion. These are designed to give users pre-prepared compliance guidelines, risk classifications and question sets instead of requiring them to draft governance policies from scratch. AI Navigator supports the full life cycle of AI oversight, from experimentation and deployment to retirement. It is being offered as a standalone SaaS product for new and existing SAS customers, who will receive free access for six months. Its launch on Microsoft Marketplace also adds to the long-running partnership between SAS and Microsoft. The software is designed to help organisations manage AI use cases across different environments, including those running on Microsoft Azure. **Healthcare testing** One early tester was Erasmus University Medical Centre in the Netherlands, which worked with SAS and Delft University of Technology on a project called the Responsible Ethical AI in Health Care Lab. Open Source AI.content: UPDATED 20:46 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Reflection AI debuts open-source Beam model with 501B parameters Reflection AI Inc. today introduced Beam, an open-source large language model with 501 billion parameters. The launch comes a few months after the startup raised funding at a $25 billion valuation. Around the same time, Reflection AI reportedly inked a $6.3 billion deal with SpaceX Corp. to rent Nvidia GB300 NVL72 appliances. It used those systems, which each contain 72 graphics cards, to train Beam. Reflection AI benchmarked its model against GLM-5.2, an open-source LLM that includes about 250 billion more parameters. The company determined that Beam can perform some tasks better while using between one third and one fourth the hardware. Furthermore, it says that the LLM approaches the performance of Qwen 3.8-Max, a model with over 2 trillion parameters. The launch is particularly notable because many of the open-source ecosystem’s most advanced LLMs were created by Chinese companies. That includes Qwen 3.8-Max and GLM-5.2. Beam is the first open-source model from a U.S. startup to have demonstrated comparable or better performance. However, free LLMs continue to trail frontier models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.1. Reflection AI kicked off the development of Beam by training a relatively small prototype model. It then created a series of successively larger, more capable algorithms. The workflow eventually produced Beam Base, the foundation on which Beam is based. Reflection AI developed Beam Base using a cluster of 6,144 graphics cards. It trained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens sourced from the public web and commercial sources. According to Reflection AI, that dataset included a significant amount of software code. The company created custom filters for each programming language to remove low-quality files. Reflection AI developed Beam Base in under four weeks. It subsequently performed midtraining, an optimization process that extended the model’s context window and enhanced its reasoning capabilities. That phase of the project set the stage for the third, most hardware-intensive phase of the training workflow. Reflection AI spun up 10,000 GB300 graphics cards and used them to launch 1.3 billion reinforcement learning sandboxes. Those are virtual environments in which an AI model learns new skills. Beam’s sandboxes were optimized for tasks such as generating code, searching the web and running AI agents. Reflection AI says that the project’s reinforcement learning phase took only four weeks. The company avoided unnecessary delays by developing software that prevented malfunctions from interrupting the workflow. According to Reflection AI, its cluster achieved a median recovery time of eight minutes across the 71 errors that cropped up during training. Beam is initially available through an early access program. Open Source AI.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Running a 125B-Parameter LLM on a Home PC: "Strata" Opens a New Frontier for Local AI [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Strata, an AI execution application released on GitHub, enables a quantized version of the 125-billion-parameter "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next" model to run on consumer-grade high-end gaming PCs. By loading the entire Mixture of Experts (MoE) model into system RAM while placing only frequently used expert models in GPU VRAM, combined with speculative decoding, the software operates with just 12GB of VRAM and 32GB of RAM. On an RTX 5070 setup, the 2-bit quantized version achieved 94 tokens per second. Strata exposes an OpenAI-compatible API on localhost, allowing existing tools to connect without modification, though degraded output quality has been reported with low-bit quantization. ##### Key Elements ![Running a 125B-Parameter LLM on a Home PC: ](https://img.biggo.com/YJjHhrfBMJ-Z7p_1apznIUsM4xcHiaGqLBDwLj1CaKs/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzM2NGIyMDFhLWJkMzQtNDE0Ny04MDZhLTExMGUwMTIxNmI4M18xNzkxMjA3MDM4X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) As large language models (LLMs) continue to improve in capability, an effort to overturn the assumption that running cutting-edge models requires data-center-class compute resources is drawing attention. Strata, an AI execution application released on GitHub, is software that enables a quantized version of the 125-billion-parameter "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next" model to run locally at high speed on relatively accessible high-end gaming PCs. Strata, published by developer Niko1221, employs a design that loads the entire MoE (Mixture of Experts) model into system RAM while placing only the most frequently used expert models into GPU VRAM. By combining this with speculative decoding—where a lightweight model predicts the next token—it enables large-scale models to run even on PCs with limited VRAM capacity. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is composed of 24,576 small expert models, of which only 10 are needed to generate each token. It helps you inspect pull requests, catch issues, and decide what deserves attention before code ships. But the quality of existing AI reviewers can be hard to measure, and you need to know the strengths of a reviewer before you know if it will help you. Some reviewers surface more issues, some produce less noise, and some are stronger at catching critical problems while others surface smaller improvements, too. You may need code review to do different things within your workflow. That makes it important to understand how reviewers actually compare: what different systems catch, what they miss, and the tradeoffs they make. A good code review benchmark should reflect the diversity of real pull requests, capture a broad set of review findings, and support meaningful breakdowns by severity, category, and precision-recall preferences. For teams building code review agents, the benchmark should also provide an offline signal that reliably tracks whether changes are likely to improve the experience in production. Existing benchmarks often make tradeoffs between label quality, coverage, and how well they represent real-world code review, leaving a gap for a rigorous and reproducible evaluation methodology that brings these pieces together. We built [**ReviewBench**](https://review-bench.ai/)**, a new code review offline benchmark**, to address that gap, and it is available for you to use today. It follows the language, repo size, and size distribution of pull requests, modeled after over 100 million real pull requests on GitHub. It uses a multi-source golden set and a consistent evaluation rubric and has been independently validated by senior engineers. Just as important, with the help of ReviewBench, our offline evaluation of Copilot code review (CCR) has become more effective at anticipating the direction of production experiments, giving us greater confidence that measured improvements reflect meaningful gains for users. Come [join our Reddit Sub](https://www.reddit.com/r/gamingonlinuxsub/) as another place to follow the community! # [System76 COSMIC projects will no longer accept LLM-generated content in code submissions](https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2026/10/system76-cosmic-projects-will-no-longer-accept-llm-generated-content-in-code-submissions/) By **[Liam Squires-Hand](https://www.gamingonlinux.com/profiles/2/)** [0 comments](#comments "Comments Link") The AI machine continues to cause problems for some developers - with System76 now banning LLM-generated content in code Pull Requests for COSMIC. In a post on Reddit, System76 Principal Engineer Jeremy Soller said: > "There are various reasons, and I don't want to hurt anybody's feelings. The primary reason is simply our team's load for reviews. In particular, we would like to prioritize working on contributions from our own team and regular contributors, while we have been receiving far more changes from first-time contributors using LLMs. These changes are often unplanned and have had a low acceptance rate. > > The policy can be seen as part of the revised PR template here: <https://github.com/pop-os/cosmic-epoch/blob/master/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md>. > > There is an exception for cosmic-flatpak, where each project manages its own flatpak manifest, pointing to its own code. These manifests are reviewed by our team for the correct sandboxing prior to accepting changes." Their [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/pop-os/pop/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) have been updated to mention "Content generated by any LLM (also known as AI) may not be contributed in issues or PRs to Pop!\_OS projects including code, comments, and descriptions". We've seen this across many open source projects, like the popular cross-platform [Godot Engine that also had issues with AI requests flooding in](https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2026/07/godot-engine-to-get-stricter-on-ai-contributed-code/). Recently we also saw the KDE team [attempt to make some LLM guidelines as well](https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2026/09/kde-developers-attempts-at-creating-llm-guidelines-are-not-going-well/). This will no doubt continue to spread due to how easy it is to access AI tools. At least until the bubble finally pops - if it ever does. Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Two former Groq engineers have filed a lawsuit in Delaware's Court of Chancery alleging that Nvidia's $20 billion asset deal with the AI chip startup unfairly squeezed out common stockholders. The complaint claims Groq's board approved the transaction without a required stockholder vote and that $17 billion of the deal value went to a non-exclusive technology license while another $3 billion was reserved for employee stock awards. Groq has called the lawsuit meritless and said it will defend itself vigorously. Nvidia has not commented on the litigation. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers](https://img.biggo.com/0wAiLEjI8NkcbWSTvFfEa_460KUCeiIqgozG7i8w6OM/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2NjMGJlMGFlLWY3ZmQtNDFjZC1iNjU3LWYzMWQ0YWExZjVmM18xNzkxMjUxMTA0X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is facing a legal challenge over its $20 billion asset agreement with AI chip designer Groq, after two former engineers at the startup alleged that stockholders were squeezed out at an unfairly low price. Joshua Rubin and Benjamin Serebrin filed the complaint on Oct. 2 in Delaware's Court of Chancery. Both had departed Groq before the Nvidia transaction was announced, according to their LinkedIn profiles, but the lawsuit states they continued to hold equity in the company. The case marks the first significant legal test of a deal structure that has drawn scrutiny for how it allocates value between technology licenses, employee compensation, and common stockholders. The dispute traces back to a December licensing agreement that granted Nvidia access to Groq's inference technology, which is used to run trained AI models efficiently. As part of that arrangement, Groq founder and CEO Jonathan Ross and President Sunny Madra joined Nvidia, along with other senior executives. The lawsuit indicates that roughly 150 to 200 Groq engineers also became Nvidia employees in connection with the transaction. Groq, for its part, has maintained that it will continue operating as an independent company and has raised approximately $1 billion since June from investors that include Nvidia itself. The core of the complaint centers on how the $20 billion was divided. The plaintiffs allege that Nvidia assigned $17 billion to a license described as non-exclusive, while another $3 billion was reserved in Nvidia restricted stock units for Groq employees who moved with the technology. The lawsuit further claims that investment funds with representatives on Groq's board were positioned to capture windfall returns from what the plaintiffs describe as a later squeeze-out transaction. "A Board majority was conflicted as a result," the complaint states, adding that "the Board's conflicted choice cost Groq's stockholders billions of dollars." The former engineers argue that Groq's directors "sold the company to Nvidia without the stockholder vote Delaware law requires and without any process designed to test or maximize the value of what Nvidia bought." Groq has forcefully rejected the allegations. A company spokesperson said the licensing agreement "delivered exceptional value for Groq, our investors, and our employees." The spokesperson added that the lawsuit "is meritless and we will vigorously defend ourselves against it," while emphasizing that the company remains focused on serving customers and building what it describes as the world's leading AI inference cloud. Infra & Chips.content: [Refrigeration Tech Hub](https://refindustry.com/about/ "About us") EN * EN English * [ES Spanish](https://refindustry.com/es/news/mitsubishi-electric-presenta-disenos-de-centros-de-datos-de-ia-chip-to-grid/) * [IT Italian](https://refindustry.com/it/news/mitsubishi-electric-presenta-i-progetti-ai-chip-to-grid-per-i-data-center/) * [DE German](https://refindustry.com/de/news/mitsubishi-electric-stellt-chip-to-grid-designs-fur-ki-rechenzentren-vor/) * [FR French](https://refindustry.com/fr/news/mitsubishi-electric-devoile-ses-architectures-de-data-centers-ia-chip-to-grid/) [Subscribe free](https://refindustry.com/subscribe/) [Sign in](https://refindustry.com/account/?mode=signin) # Mitsubishi Electric Releases Chip-to-Grid AI Data Center Designs The architecture integrates AC and 800VDC distribution, on-site generation, battery storage and dual-loop cooling for high-density AI loads. ![Mitsubishi Electric Releases Chip-to-Grid AI Data Center Designs](https://refindustry.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/data-center1-1024x691.jpg) Mitsubishi Electric announced Chip-to-Grid DSX reference designs for U.S. data centers deploying NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and future AI infrastructure. Released through Mitsubishi Electric Power Products, the designs coordinate grid connection, on-site power, chip-level power supply and cooling, with support for data centers scaling toward gigawatt-class electrical demand. The architecture combines power transmission and distribution equipment with data center power supply and cooling systems. It supports both conventional 415/480VAC distribution and 800VDC distribution inside the data center, providing configurations for current infrastructure as well as higher-voltage DC architectures associated with dense AI computing installations. Sites using the reference designs can incorporate on-site power generation and battery energy storage systems. During normal operation, these resources are intended to reduce reliance on the utility grid; during a grid outage, the facility can switch to autonomous operation through its own microgrid. The configuration is intended to maintain power stability while supporting the electrical requirements of large AI data centers. Cooling is based on a dual-loop architecture combining direct liquid cooling for chips with air cooling for other equipment. The arrangement targets high-density AI loads and integrates facility cooling with the broader power system rather than treating thermal management as a separate infrastructure layer. The reference designs are intended to support NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI system, which integrates 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs, as well as later NVIDIA AI infrastructure. Mitsubishi Electric plans to use the designs as a basis for developing integrated data center offerings that combine power generation, energy storage, transmission and distribution, chip power delivery and cooling. Infra & Chips.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Vertiv wins NVIDIA DSX Ready cooling qualification](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/05/Vertiv__CoolChip_CDU_2300-story-320577.webp) [DataCentre infrastructure](https://itbrief.asia/tag/datacentre-infrastructure) [Hyperscale](https://itbrief.asia/tag/hyperscale) [Edge Computing](https://itbrief.asia/tag/edge-computing) # Vertiv wins NVIDIA DSX Ready cooling qualification Mon, 5th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Sean Mitchell](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](/author/sean-mitchell) Vertiv's 2.3 MW CoolChip coolant distribution unit has qualified as an NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU, making it the first coolant distribution unit to receive that qualification under the NVIDIA DSX Ready programme. The designation applies to a model in Vertiv's liquid-to-liquid CDU range for high-density computing environments. A coolant distribution unit manages the flow and temperature of liquid used to remove heat from computing systems. Vertiv's 2.3 MW model supports direct-to-chip and rear-door heat exchanger applications and is designed for installation either at the end of a row or along the room perimeter. The qualification comes as data centre operators and equipment suppliers adapt to AI workloads, which are driving up rack densities and putting more pressure on power and cooling systems. Amazon could collect billions of dollars for AI chips and continue using those same chips to serve customers. That is the logic behind a reported proposal to transfer approximately $8 billion of Nvidia hardware to an investment vehicle then lease it back. The attraction is immediate cash. The price is a stream of future payments whose terms will determine whether the transaction creates value. Let’s break down what has been reported, why Amazon would consider this financing structure and how to assess the economics beyond the headline. We’ll examine its cash flow, AWS profitability, GPU rental prices and valuation before considering the implications for US and Indian investors. Our assessment is that the proposal is understandable in a period of exceptional infrastructure spending. Its financial merit depends on the cash actually released, the cost of continued access and the risks Amazon retains. As of October 5, the public reporting describes discussions rather than a completed transaction. ## **What is Amazon’s proposed $8 billion Nvidia deal?** The Financial Times reported the proposal on October 2. Reuters subsequently reported that Amazon had been discussing investor interest in a special-purpose vehicle (SPV) that would hold thousands of Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips. Amazon would lease the hardware back while the vehicle raised outside financing. An SPV is a separate legal entity created for a defined transaction. Here, its purpose would be to connect investors supplying capital with equipment that Amazon continues to use.
